<hypothesis>
The research hypothesis.

kind: hypothesis
title: Temperature Flattens Ideas, Context Reorders Them
hypothesis: >-
  When an instruction-tuned open-weight LLM (>=1B parameters) is asked an open design task such as 'implement a path search
  algorithm', which solution idea it picks (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, A*, bidirectional, ...) works like a discrete choice. That
  choice is made at a few early COMMITMENT TOKENS, and at those tokens the residual stream carries a readable IDEA-UTILITY
  VECTOR u: one score per candidate idea, read from the logits or the logit lens at the commitment position, or from a linear
  probe on the state just before it. This vector, together with the similarity geometry of the ideas' internal representations,
  PREDICTS BEFORE GENERATION what each 'creativity knob' will do. Each knob acts on a different parameter of one random-utility
  model. (1) TEMPERATURE only rescales u. Idea log-odds therefore fall on straight Arrhenius lines, ln[P_T(j)/P_T(mode)] ~
  -(u_mode - u_j)/T, with slopes equal to the internal utility gaps. Temperature can flatten the idea distribution but never
  reorder it, and phrasing diversity grows far faster than idea diversity: the user's case (a) '1 idea x many phrasings',
  and with top-k=10 a hard ceiling equal to the number of idea tokens inside the top-k at the commitment position. (2) RANDOM
  CONTEXT SEEDS ('seed=d32qxk4nt43', '(horse chair roof love)') act as random utility shocks with a measurable internal spread
  sigma_seed. They change the chosen idea only when sigma_seed is comparable to the utility gap, which explains why seeding
  fails on canonical tasks like weighted shortest path -> Dijkstra. (3) BANS restrict the choice set but break the independence
  of irrelevant alternatives (IIA): the banned idea's probability flows mainly to its nearest neighbours in the model's internal
  idea geometry, as in a nested logit, rather than to the remaining ideas in proportion to their base rates. 'Banning the
  attractor creates an adjacent attractor', e.g. Dijkstra -> SPFA. (4) NOVELTY INSTRUCTIONS shift u along a single typicality
  axis. The 'default answer' is therefore the MODE of the internal utility landscape, not an average of possible answers,
  and only interventions that change u (context, or direct steering at the commitment layer) can reorder ideas or reach ones
  outside the usual menu.
motivation: >-
  People reach for temperature as the 'creativity knob' and for 'be original'/'don't use X' prompts as the novelty lever.
  Behavioral studies, though, show that temperature mostly adds surface variation (Peeperkorn et al. 2024), that incidental
  cues swing algorithm choice by up to 100 percentage points with no mechanism identified (Invisible Lottery, 2026), and that
  banning the dominant solution simply produces a new dominant one: the DrejcPesjak/llm-creativity repo saw 16 of 25 programs
  collapse to SPFA under a ban list, while random seeds had zero effect. Nobody has a model that PREDICTS these outcomes,
  so practitioners tune knobs blindly. If idea choice is a readable discrete choice, one internal measurement (the utility
  vector and the idea geometry at the commitment token) tells you in advance: whether temperature can reach a new idea at
  a tolerable temperature (only if the gap is small), whether seeding will do anything (only if sigma_seed is comparable to
  the gap), and where a ban will send the model (to the banned idea's neighbour, not to something novel). It also says what
  WILL produce new ideas: acting on u directly at the commitment point. That turns the folk question 'is the LLM just giving
  me the average answer?' into a measurable claim (mode of a utility landscape, not a mean) and turns creativity control from
  prompt lore into a predictable intervention. It also directly answers the user's questions (a)/(b)/(c) about temperature
  and top-k, the seeding question, the 'average answer' question, and the 'ban the top-5: does mass move to the edge or the
  opposite side of the manifold?' question.
assumptions:
- >-
  For algorithm-design prompts, the idea is fixed within the first few dozen generated tokens, typically at an algorithm-name
  token in the preamble ('Here is an implementation of A*') or at a data-structure token (deque vs heapq vs a stack/recursion).
  Forking-path resampling (Bigelow et al. 2025) can locate this point, so a per-sample commitment position exists for most
  samples.
- >-
  Generated solutions can be classified reliably into idea classes with a deterministic AST/keyword classifier (deque+popleft
  -> BFS, heapq without a heuristic -> Dijkstra, heapq plus a heuristic -> A*, explicit stack or recursion -> DFS, repeated
  edge relaxation -> Bellman-Ford/SPFA, two frontiers -> bidirectional, otherwise 'other/novel'), checked by running the code
  on random graphs against an oracle, as in the llm-creativity repo.
- >-
  Mid-layer residual representations of the commitment window, meaning the mean over the commitment token plus the next ~16
  tokens, give a stable, seed-robust geometry of ideas (centroid cosine similarities). This geometry is computed ONLY from
  unbanned baseline runs, so it can predict substitution under bans out of sample.
- >-
  The instruction-tuned models used are not so mode-collapsed that the baseline menu has only one idea. At T=1, at least 3
  idea classes occur with >=3% frequency on at least 2 of the 3 tasks; this is checked in the first screening step, and tasks
  failing it are swapped.
- >-
  GPU inference is available for the experiment phase (a single 24-48 GB GPU via the aii-runpod skill; the local machine has
  2 CPU cores and no GPU). vLLM handles sampling and HuggingFace/TransformerLens with forward hooks handles activations. CPU
  fallback: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, outputs capped at 160 tokens (enough to classify the idea, since commitment is early),
  n=40 per cell.
investigation_approach: |-
  MODELS: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct (primary) and gemma-2-2b-it (second family; has public Gemma Scope SAEs for feature-level naming). Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct is optional for replication. TASKS (3): T1 'Implement a path search algorithm in Python' (open menu), T2 'Implement a sorting algorithm' (large menu: quick/merge/heap/insertion/radix/counting/shell/...), T3 'Implement a function that finds a shortest path in a weighted graph' (the canonical Dijkstra attractor, as in the repo). Same base seed everywhere, as the user asked.

  PHASE 1, BEHAVIOR (the user's a/b/c questions). Grid: T in {0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0, 1.3, 1.6} x top-k in {10, none}, n=100 samples per cell per task. Classify each sample's idea, run its code against an oracle on 50 random graphs/arrays, and measure phrasing diversity within each idea (normalized-code edit distance and embedding distance). Partition diversity ecologically: Hill numbers between ideas (beta) vs within ideas (alpha). This answers (a) vs (b) vs (c) directly. Conditions: baseline; 'Make a new algorithm'; 'Make a fully novel algorithm never seen before... 2000 words'; 3 random-character seeds and 3 random-word seeds x 30 seed strings each; bans of the top-1/top-3/top-5 baseline ideas; and a control ban of a rare idea (tests priming, cf. Semantic Gravity Wells). Bans run at T=0.7, n=100.

  PHASE 2, LOCATE THE CHOICE. For 60 baseline samples per task, run forking-path resampling: at each of the first 64 positions, resample 10 continuations and classify them. The commitment token is the first position after which the idea distribution stays fixed. Then test a probe and the logit lens: at each layer, does the residual stream at the commitment token, and at the prompt-final token, linearly predict the final idea? This gives the layer and position where the choice forms. Causal check: patch the commitment-token residual from a BFS run into a Dijkstra run at the identified layers and measure the idea flip rate (with a random-position patch as control).

  PHASE 3, READ THE CHOICE MODEL (all from baseline runs only). u = log-probabilities at the commitment position over each idea's identifying tokens, cross-checked with a multinomial probe on the pre-commitment residual. Geometry S = cosine similarity between idea centroids of commitment-window activations at the best probe layer. Draw the 'path-search algorithm manifold' the user asked for: PCA/UMAP of the activations, centroids sized by count, then the same plot after bans with arrows showing where mass moved.

  PHASE 4, PREDICT EVERY KNOB OUT OF SAMPLE. (i) Temperature: fit an Arrhenius line per idea and correlate its slope with the internal gap u_mode-u_j. Predicted top-k ceiling = the number of idea tokens in the top-k at commitment. Count rank reversals. (ii) Seeds: measure sigma_seed as the spread of u across seed prefixes. Predicted greedy flip rate = P(argmax changes under Gaussian shocks of size sigma_seed), compared with the observed rate on each task. (iii) Bans: compare three predictors of the post-ban idea distribution: IIA-proportional renormalization of the baseline; behavioral co-occurrence similarity; and a geometry nested logit P'(j) proportional to P(j) * (1 + lambda * sum_banned b of S_jb * P(b)), where lambda is fitted on one task and tested on the other two. Score them by Jensen-Shannon divergence and held-out log-likelihood. Edge vs opposite side: check whether post-ban mass sits closer in S to the banned centroids than the baseline-weighted average does. (iv) Novelty instructions: regress the shift in u on log baseline frequency to get a single 'typicality' slope.

  PHASE 5, INFLUENCE IT. At the commitment layer and position, add a steering vector built from the utility-probe weights that FLATTENS u (an internal version of 'generate the menu, then pick at random'). Also test projecting out the subspace spanned by the menu-idea centroids, which aims for ideas outside the menu. Compare against temperature, bans and seeds at matched pass rate on idea entropy, outside-menu share and correctness. Name the features involved with Gemma Scope SAE latents on gemma-2-2b-it (e.g. 'priority queue', 'level-order') and list which ones the steering moves.

  COST: roughly 20k generations of <=400 tokens (about 1-2 GPU-hours with vLLM on a 3B model) plus about 4k activation-cached forward passes and about 40k forking-path rollouts of 64 tokens (about 1-2 GPU-hours). No paid LLM calls are needed, since classification is rule-based with code execution.
success_criteria: >-
  CONFIRM if most of the following hold on both models. (1) Commitment is localized: for >=75% of samples the idea is fixed
  within the first 48 generated tokens, and patching the commitment-token residual flips the idea in >=50% of trials vs <10%
  for a random-position patch. (2) Temperature law: the Arrhenius fits ln-odds vs 1/T reach R^2>=0.85 for ideas with >=3%
  frequency at T=1; the slopes correlate with the internal gaps u_mode-u_j (Spearman >=0.7); there are no rank reversals among
  the top-3 ideas for T<=1.3; within-idea phrasing diversity rises >=3x more steeply with T than idea count; and with top-k=10
  the number of distinct ideas never exceeds the predicted ceiling. (3) Seeds: the shock model predicts the per-task flip
  rate within +/-0.10, and seeds are ineffective (<5% flips) exactly on tasks where gap/sigma_seed>3 (expected for T3). (4)
  Bans: the geometry nested logit beats IIA-proportional renormalization by >=20% lower Jensen-Shannon divergence on held-out
  tasks and bans; in >=70% of single bans the top substitute is the banned idea's nearest internal neighbour; and post-ban
  mass lies on the 'edge' (closer to the banned centroids than the baseline average is). (5) Influence: commitment-point flattening
  at least doubles idea entropy relative to the best temperature at equal pass rate (>=80% pass), while bans mostly reshuffle
  within the menu (outside-menu share <15%). DISCONFIRM / redirect: curved Arrhenius plots or rank reversals with rising T
  would mean commitment is spread over many tokens and ideas reachable by many paths gain at high T (alternate A1). Geometry
  predicting no better than IIA would mean bans redistribute proportionally (the choice set is unstructured). Post-ban mass
  moving AWAY from the banned centroids would mean ban-induced repulsion through shared features (alternate A3). Each of these
  is still an informative mechanistic finding about how the knobs act.
related_works:
- >-
  DrejcPesjak/llm-creativity (GitHub, 2026): behavioral study of one weighted shortest-path task with claude-sonnet-5. Seeds
  had no effect; a negative-memory ban list pushed 16/25 programs to SPFA ('banning the attractor creates a new one'); 'selection
  is the bottleneck'. It uses a closed model with uncontrolled temperature and does no internal analysis. We use its findings
  as phenomena to PREDICT from internal utilities and geometry.
- >-
  The Invisible Lottery: How Subtle Cues Steer Algorithm Choice in LLM Code Generation (arXiv 2606.04057): 46k runs showing
  that incidental cues shift algorithm-family distributions by up to 100 pp, with temperature sweeps. Purely behavioral: it
  has a token log-probability diagnostic 'without identifying a mechanism' and leaves activation patching and causal mediation
  to future work. It does not cover bans, substitution structure, or prediction of knob effects. We provide the internal choice
  model that predicts such shifts.
- >-
  Forking Paths in Neural Text Generation (Bigelow et al., ICLR 2025): resamples tokens along a path to find forks where outcomes
  diverge. We use it as an instrument to locate commitment tokens. Our contribution is the idea-level utility readout at those
  forks and its use to predict temperature, seed and ban effects quantitatively.
- >-
  Manifold Steering (Wurgaft et al., arXiv 2605.05115; Goodfire): shows that activation manifolds mirror behavior manifolds
  (weekdays, months) and that steering along the manifold beats linear steering. Their concepts have known cyclic structure
  and no choice-set restriction. We use the geometry of solution ideas to predict where probability goes when ideas are prohibited
  (an IIA test), which has not been studied.
- >-
  Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire (arXiv 2601.08070): logit lens and patching show that naming a
  forbidden word primes it, causing violations. It studies whether the banned item leaks, not where probability goes instead.
  Our ban analysis concerns the substitution structure among the remaining ideas, with a rare-idea ban as a priming control.
- >-
  The Innate Economic Preferences of Language Models (Buchanan & Foster, arXiv 2607.26288): notes that LLM generation is isomorphic
  to a random-utility model and finds IIA violations across prompts in portfolio choices. It does not cover idea generation,
  commitment tokens, representation geometry, or a mapping of creativity knobs onto choice-model parameters. The RUM framing
  itself is not our novelty; reading it from internals at the commitment point and using it to predict knob effects is.
- >-
  Is Temperature the Creativity Parameter of LLMs? (Peeperkorn et al., 2024) and NAACL 2025 hypothesis-generation work: show
  behaviorally that temperature weakly raises novelty and that idea diversity saturates. We offer a mechanism and a quantitative
  law (Arrhenius slopes = internal utility gaps; top-k ceiling) that explains why.
- >-
  Intent Factored Generation (Ahmed et al., ICML 2025), String Seed of Thought (Sakana, ICLR 2026), Verbalized Sampling (2025):
  prompt-level two-stage or seed-based diversity methods. They act externally. Our Phase-5 intervention is an internal equivalent
  at the commitment point, and our seed analysis predicts WHEN naive seeding works (sigma_seed vs gap) instead of engineering
  around it.
- >-
  Emergent Response Planning in LLMs (arXiv 2502.06258): probes on the prompt representation predict response attributes.
  We go beyond decodability to a causal, idea-level utility vector at the commitment token whose geometry predicts counterfactual
  (banned or seeded) behavior.
inspiration: >-
  Econometrics, specifically McFadden's random-utility discrete-choice theory, transferred at the METHODOLOGICAL level. In
  that framework each intervention maps to a distinct parameter: the logit scale parameter (temperature), random utility shocks
  (seeds), choice-set restriction with the IIA / Hausman-McFadden test and nested-logit substitution (bans), and attribute
  coefficients (a typicality penalty for 'be novel' instructions). The nests, normally specified by hand, are read off the
  model's own representation geometry. The red-bus/blue-bus problem is exactly the user's 'ban the top 5: edge or opposite
  side?' question. Physical chemistry supplied the Arrhenius plot, ln(rate) vs 1/T with slope = barrier, as the diagnostic
  separating single-barrier commitment (straight lines) from multi-pathway (entropic) commitment (curved lines, rank reversals).
  Ecology supplied the alpha/beta diversity partition (Hill numbers within vs between ideas), which formalizes the user's
  (a)/(b)/(c) '10 ideas x 1 phrasing vs 1 idea x 10 phrasings' question. Finally, the llm-creativity repo's empirical puzzles
  (seeds inert, bans create a new attractor, selection is the bottleneck) motivated looking for one internal object that predicts
  all three.
terms:
- term: Idea class
  definition: >-
    The solution approach a generated program implements (e.g. BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, A*, bidirectional search, Bellman-Ford/SPFA,
    or 'other/novel'), assigned by a deterministic code classifier and checked by execution.
- term: Commitment token
  definition: >-
    The first generated position after which resampling the rest of the output no longer changes the idea class. Found by
    forking-path resampling.
- term: Idea-utility vector (u)
  definition: >-
    One score per idea class, read at the commitment token: the model's log-probability of each idea's identifying token(s),
    or a linear probe's logits on the residual stream just before commitment. It plays the role of 'utilities' in a discrete-choice
    model.
- term: Random-utility / discrete-choice model
  definition: >-
    An economics model in which a chooser picks the option with the highest utility plus random noise. The multinomial logit
    version gives softmax choice probabilities with a scale (temperature) parameter.
- term: IIA (independence of irrelevant alternatives)
  definition: >-
    Property of the plain logit: removing one option redistributes its probability to the others in proportion to their existing
    shares. Violations mean substitution is structured by similarity.
- term: Nested logit / geometry-weighted substitution
  definition: >-
    A choice model in which similar options substitute for each other more strongly. Here the similarity comes from cosine
    similarity between idea centroids in the model's activations, computed on unbanned runs.
- term: Arrhenius plot
  definition: >-
    A plot of log-odds (or log-rate) against 1/temperature. Straight lines mean one fixed barrier (here, a fixed internal
    utility gap); curvature means several competing pathways.
- term: Seed shock (sigma_seed)
  definition: >-
    How much irrelevant random context prepended to the prompt moves the internal utility vector, measured as its spread across
    seed strings. Seeding can only change the idea when this is comparable to the utility gap.
- term: Alpha/beta diversity (Hill numbers)
  definition: >-
    Ecological diversity split into within-group (phrasings within one idea) and between-group (number and evenness of distinct
    ideas) components.
- term: Outside-menu share
  definition: >-
    Fraction of correct solutions that fall into no known idea class: the operational measure of a genuinely novel solution.
summary: >-
  An LLM's choice of solution idea (BFS vs Dijkstra vs A*) is a discrete choice made at a few early commitment tokens, governed
  by an internal utility vector and idea geometry that can be read before generation. These predict that temperature only
  flattens and never reorders ideas, that seeds work only when their internal shock beats the utility gap, and that bans send
  probability to the banned idea's internal neighbours (an IIA violation) rather than toward novelty. Steering the utilities
  at the commitment point is then the real creativity knob.
alternates:
- title: Ideas form gradually, so heat can reorder
  hypothesis: >-
    Idea choice is NOT made at a single commitment token. It builds up over the first sentences or lines through many partially
    committing tokens, so an idea's probability is a sum over many paths. Raising temperature then systematically favours
    'entropic' ideas, those reachable through many low-probability routes such as generic search skeletons that drift into
    DFS or 'other', over 'energetic' ideas with one sharp high-probability path such as canonical Dijkstra. The result is
    curved Arrhenius plots and rank reversals at T>1 that are predicted by each idea's path multiplicity measured at low T.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    This wins if the forking-path analysis shows idea mass spread over many positions rather than one fork, which is plausible
    for chatty instruct models that write a plan before coding. Temperature would then be a weak but real reordering knob
    whose direction is predictable from path multiplicity rather than from a single utility gap.
- title: Bans push ideas to the far side
  hypothesis: >-
    Prohibiting the top ideas in the prompt suppresses the internal features they share with their neighbours. Probability
    therefore flows AWAY from the banned region of the idea manifold, to ideas on the opposite side such as Bellman-Ford or
    IDA* after banning BFS/Dijkstra/A*, not to the banned ideas' nearest neighbours. The displacement distance grows with
    how many features the banned ideas share, measured by Gemma Scope SAE latent overlap.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    This wins if the suppression signal the instruction creates (cf. Semantic Gravity Wells' 22.8-point suppression in successful
    cases) acts on shared features rather than on the specific idea token, so neighbours are suppressed along with the banned
    idea. That is likelier for larger bans (top-5) and for models with strong instruction following, and it would make bans
    a surprisingly effective novelty lever.
- title: Erase the menu, not the answer
  hypothesis: >-
    Novel, correct solutions are reachable in one pass by projecting the commitment-layer residual off the low-dimensional
    subspace spanned by the known-idea centroids (linear concept erasure of the 'menu'). The model then produces correct algorithms
    outside the menu (hybrids, unusual frontier policies) at several times the rate achieved by prompt bans, 'be novel' instructions
    or temperature, at matched correctness. Prompt bans fail because naming the banned ideas re-activates the menu subspace.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    This wins if the menu occupies a compact subspace whose removal leaves task understanding (graph traversal, correctness)
    intact, so the model falls back on less typical but still competent compositions. The main hypothesis's flattening steering
    would then only reshuffle probability within the menu, while erasure would be the real route to novelty.
- title: One shared 'unusualness' dial
  hypothesis: >-
    Novelty instructions ('make a fully novel algorithm never seen before') work through a single task-general typicality
    direction in the residual stream that penalizes each idea in proportion to its baseline log-frequency. A difference-in-means
    vector extracted from novelty vs plain prompts on OTHER tasks (sorting, string search) transfers to path search and moves
    probability toward low-frequency ideas monotonically with steering strength, with no prompt change at all.
  why_it_could_win: >-
    This wins if 'typicality' is represented as a frequency-like scalar the model reads off for any task (like the persona
    or confidence directions found elsewhere) rather than as idea-specific features. Creativity would then have a single portable
    internal knob, which the main hypothesis's task-specific utility readout does not provide; CreativityNeuro's failed activation-steering
    transfer is the evidence against it.
</hypothesis>

FULL EVIDENCE BASE: All 1 research artifacts across all iterations.

--- Item 1 ---
id: art_aSN7z8WuA7Ir
type: experiment
title: Can internal knobs beat temperature for novel code?
summary: >-
  INFLUENCE ARM, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, one HF engine for every condition (per-sample seeded inverse-CDF sampler, code-block
  stop, 768 max tokens). Tasks: T1 open path search, T3 weighted shortest path. Correctness = sandboxed oracle on 50 fixed
  graphs (all must pass); idea label = AST classifier (audited vs blind gpt-4.1-mini judge on 200 programs: agreement 0.715,
  kappa 0.68). Baseline T=0.7 n=300: T1 BFS 205/DFS 80 (pass 0.70), T3 Dijkstra 225/BFS-relax 71 (pass 0.37); menus T1={bfs,dfs},
  T3={dijkstra,bfs}. Probes at gen1..8 are at chance (boilerplate opening; algorithm name first appears at median token 23.5/46.5),
  so fallback F4 was used: probe on mean(gen1..32) (bal acc ~0.65-0.69 vs shuffled 0.42), hook window prompt-final+gen1..64,
  band layers 29-31. Sweep n=150/setting (controls 75): H-probe/H-dim (5 calibrated alphas), A3 rank-1 projection + LEACE,
  A4 cross-task unusualness direction, matched-norm random controls, temperature 1.0-2.0, top-k, 'new'/'novel2000' prompts,
  ban-top-3, generate-then-select; held-out re-draw (seeds 1000..1099) for selected settings. RESULT: no internal knob survives
  the pre-registered rules -> 'prompting ceiling'. Pooled pass/idea-entropy: baseline 0.53/1.05; ban-top-3 0.43/1.59 (best
  eligible, tops entropy front); gen-then-select 0.26/2.56; best H-dim 0.57/1.06 (held-out entropy ratio vs best temperature
  0.93 T1, 1.20 T3; needed >=2; CI vs random direction includes 0); H-probe has no setting at matched pass rate; A4 dial not
  monotone (Spearman 0.49 T1, -0.26 T3) although its readout transfers (AUROC 1.0); judge-confirmed novel-and-correct share
  = 0 in every condition (all 70 rule-'other' passing programs were known algorithms), so A3 fails despite LEACE erasing idea
  decodability offline (T3 0.88->0.35). Mechanistic finding: H directions SELECT rather than flatten (H-dim a=0.224 turns
  T1 into DFS 145/150 at unchanged pass 0.68) - internal knobs give controllable choice among known ideas, not novelty; random
  matched-norm directions raise entropy about as much as targeted knobs. Noise floor: batch-composition re-run flips 11-17%
  of labels. Independent re-derivation (verify_headline.py: own oracle runner 147/147 agreement, coarse classifier 97%, pandas
  recomputation) reproduces headline numbers; placebo CIs include 0. Files: method_out.json (exp_gen_sol_out, 300 examples,
  all metrics in metadata), results/results.json (survival, CIs, Pareto, manipulation checks), figs/, gens/, scored/, judge/;
  vectors/ (vectors.pt + leace_T1/T3.pt) published; acts/ (split into <100 MB parts, src/acts_io.py) and caps/ kept on the
  run volume only.
workspace_path: >-
  /ai-inventor/aii_data/runs/run_wfWEMjpWKygr/3_invention_loop/iter_1/gen_art/gen_art_experiment_3
out_expected_files:
- method.py
- full_method_out.json
- mini_method_out.json
- preview_method_out.json
- reproducibility.md
</all_artifacts>

<figure_instructions>
THE REPORT'S FIGURES ARE CHARTS OF THIS RUN'S OWN NUMBERS. Nothing else. Every figure here is
rendered deterministically by the aii-data-fig-gen skill from the values you supply, so each bar
is exactly the height of its number and a reader can check the figure against the table beside
it. There is no image model in this document and no `figure_type` to choose: the schema takes
data figures only. Conceptual artwork, architecture drawings and flow diagrams belong to the
publishable paper, which is written later and separately.

WHAT BECOMES A FIGURE, AND WHAT DOES NOT:
  - A chart, when the point is a SHAPE the eye reads faster than the digits: a trend over a
    sweep, a gap between conditions, a distribution, a trade-off front, a confusion matrix, an
    ablation delta.
  - A MARKDOWN TABLE, when the point is the values themselves. Tabular data stays a table. A
    four-row result table redrawn as a chart loses the exact numbers and gains nothing.
  - Nothing at all, when neither: not every iteration earns a figure, and an empty one costs the
    reader a page turn.

FIGURE FORMAT: put a [FIGURE:fig_id] marker in the report text where the chart belongs — inside the
iteration section that produced its numbers, next to the table or the paragraph it settles — and
give the full spec in the separate `figures` structured-output array. Every id in the array
matches a marker in the text, and every marker matches an id in the array or in
<previous_figures>.

Set `aspect_ratio` per figure: 16:9 for side-by-side comparisons and multi-panel results, 4:3
for dense charts, 1:1 for heatmaps / confusion matrices / scatter plots, 21:9 for a long timeline
or a wide many-category bar chart.

Example in the report text:

[FIGURE:fig3]

The sweep in Table 2 shows..."

The algorithmic idea is labelled by an AST classifier, which was audited\nagainst a blind LLM judge.\n\n## Headline (pre-registered rules, `results/rules.json`)\n\n**Prompting ceiling: no internal knob survives.**\n\n| condition (pooled T1+T3, seeds 0..149) | oracle pass | idea entropy (bits) |\n|---|---|---|\n| baseline T=0.7 | 0.53 | 1.05 |\n| temperature 1.0 / 1.3 / 1.6 / 2.0 | 0.42 / 0.19 / 0.00 / 0.00 | 1.22 / 1.33 / – / – |\n| prompt \"Make a new algorithm.\" | 0.55 | 1.05 |\n| prompt \"fully novel … 2000 words\" | 0.08 | 2.20 |\n| **prompt ban top-3 ideas** (best eligible) | 0.43 | **1.59** |\n| generate-then-select (list 10, seeded pick) | 0.26 | 2.56 |\n| best H-dim (α=0.05) | 0.57 | 1.06 |\n| best A4 \"unusualness\" dial (α=0.356) | 0.47 | 1.37 |\n| A3 erasure (rank-1 projection a=0.25 / LEACE a=0.5) | 0.55 / 0.52 | 1.06 / 0.94 |\n\n* **H-flatten fails.** On the held-out draw (seeds 1000..1099), H-dim reaches 0.93× the entropy of the best\n  eligible temperature on T1 and 1.20× on T3; the rule required ≥2×. H-probe has no setting at the matched pass rate.\n* **The H directions select an idea rather than flatten the choice.** With two dominant ideas the\n  \"flatten\" direction overshoots the uniform point. The internal knob is a reliable, correctness-preserving *selector* of known ideas, not a\n  generator of new ones.\n* **A3 fails.** Judge-confirmed novel-and-correct programs: **0 in every condition**. Probes on mean(gen1..32) reach about 0.65–0.69\n  balanced accuracy, against 0.42 for within-task shuffled labels. Decodability is flat across layers, which\n  points to a readout of the name tokens rather than an early plan. The steering window was therefore widened to\n  prompt-final + gen1..64, and the band chosen by the pre-registered rule is layers 29–31.\n* **Noise floor.** Re-generating the baseline in mixed batches (`crn_rerun`) flips 17% (T1) and 11% (T3) of idea labels,\n  because bf16 batch numerics differ by batch composition. Common random numbers therefore pair conditions only\n  approximately, and no paired effect is claimed below that floor.\n* **Classifier audit.** 200 stratified programs, rule vs blind judge (gpt-4.1-mini): agreement 0.715, Cohen's\n  κ = 0.68 (≥ 0.6, so the rule labels stand). The main confusion is rule `spfa` vs judge `bfs` (queue relaxation\n  without in-queue tracking).\n\nSurvival verdicts and every CI are in `results/results.json` (`survival`, `settings.*.tasks.*.ci`,\n`knob_vs_random_controls`, `manipulation_checks`). The figures are in `figs/`.\n\n## Layout\n\n| path | content |\n|---|---|\n| `method.py` | pipeline entry point. Stages: `baseline acts probes vectors calib sweep select heldout judge analyze` (+ `explore`, post-hoc) |\n| `protocol/prompts.py`, `protocol/protocol.json` | shared protocol: task prompts, output contracts, condition texts, taxonomy |\n| `protocol/classifier.py` | AST classifier; docstrings and comments are stripped before the rules run |\n| `protocol/oracle.py` | sandboxed execution oracle: 50 graphs with seed 12345, 5 s CPU, 1 GB RAM, module-level demo code removed |\n| `src/engine.py` | the single HF engine: per-sample seeded inverse-CDF sampler, code-block stop, steering and capture hooks |\n| `src/settings.py` | registry of every condition |\n| `src/acts_io.py` | split activation cache: writer and lazy memory-mapped reader |\n| `src/probes.py`, `src/vectors.py` | idea probes; H-probe, H-dim, A3 bases, LEACE, A4 direction and random controls |\n| `src/analysis.py` | metrics, bootstrap CIs, survival rules, OpenRouter judge, figures, `method_out.json` |\n| `verify_headline.py` | independent re-derivation (own classifier, own oracle runner, pandas) plus placebo tests → `results/verify_headline.json` |\n| `score_backlog.py` | recovery: scores generations that were left unscored |\n| `run_post.sh` | the post-sweep chain that was actually run |\n| `tests/` | classifier/oracle unit tests (`tests/refs/`), engine tests (sampler, hooks), `test_acts_split.py` (split-cache readers) |\n| `gens/{T1,T3}/*.jsonl` | every generation: prompt, text, seed, sampler and intervention spec |\n| `scored/{T1,T3}/*.jsonl` | label, oracle pass, fraction correct, degeneration flags; `oracle_cache.jsonl` |\n| `judge/` | judge verdicts (`verdicts.jsonl`), audit sample, cost (`cost.json`, $0.081 in total) |\n| `results/` | `context.json` (menus, band, alphas), `probe_curve.json`, `calibration.json`, `rules.json`, `vector_checks.json`, `heldout_plan.json`, `results.json`, `verify_headline.json` |\n| `figs/` | probe curve, Pareto fronts (entropy, off-menu, novel), violin of fraction correct, A4 dose-response, idea shares, PCA \"manifold\" view |\n| `method_out.json` (+ `full_`, `mini_`, `preview_`) | schema `exp_gen_sol_out`: 300 examples (T1/T3 × seeds 0..149) with baseline and per-method generations, plus all metrics in `metadata` |\n| `acts/` | cached baseline residuals, 0.9 GB, split into `baseline_{T1,T3}_part_001..006.npy` (50 samples each, 73 MB) and read through `src/acts_io.py`. **Kept on the run's volume only**; not in the published repo |\n| `caps/` | residuals captured during steered generation, 0.9 GB. **Kept on the run's volume only** |\n| `vectors/vectors.pt`, `vectors/leace_{T1,T3}.pt` | every intervention vector and probe weight (0.6 MB); LEACE erasers stored per task (50 MB each) so each file is under 100 MB |\n\n## How to run\n\n```bash\nuv venv .venv --python=3.12 && uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.lock.txt\nexport PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True\n.venv/bin/python method.py baseline   # 600 gens\n.venv/bin/python method.py acts && .venv/bin/python method.py probes --workers 20\n.venv/bin/python method.py vectors && .venv/bin/python method.py calib --batch 200\n.venv/bin/python method.py sweep --batch 200 --n_main 150 --n_ctrl 75\n./run_post.sh                          # judge -> select -> heldout -> judge -> analyze\n.venv/bin/python method.py explore --batch 200 --n_main 150   # post-hoc, excluded from survival\n.venv/bin/python method.py judge && .venv/bin/python method.py analyze\n.venv/bin/python verify_headline.py\n```\n\nSee `reproducibility.md` for the exact sequence, the hardware used and the runtimes.\n\n## Deviations from the plan (all recorded)\n\n* **F4 applied**: probes use mean(gen1..32) and the hook window is prompt-final + gen1..64, because gen1..8 probes\n  are at chance.\n* **Menus exclude `other`**: T1 = {BFS, DFS} and T3 = {Dijkstra, BFS}, so k = 2 and A3 has rank 1 only.\n* **Oracle runs only the requested code**: it executes imports, defs and safe assignments. Module-level demo code\n  crashed 22% of T3 programs for reasons unrelated to the algorithm.\n* **Code-block early stop (F1 rule)**: applied to every condition.\n* **Larger samples**: n = 150 per setting and 75 per control, up from the planned 100/50; the held-out draw is\n  100 seeds.\n* **Allocator change**: after 2,400 generations the sweep was restarted with\n  `PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True`, an allocator-only change, and resumed from the files.\n* **Post-hoc low-α H settings**: `Hprobe_x_*` and `Hdim_x_0.075` (`explore`) are reported, but they are not used\n  by the survival rules.\n* **Single model**: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct only, and all results are single-model.\n\n## Restoring removed files\n\nOnly `.venv/` is marked `delete` in `.aii/manifest.yaml`. To recreate it with the pinned versions:\n\n```bash\nuv venv .venv --python=3.12\nuv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.lock.txt\n```\n\nThe model weights are not stored here. They are downloaded on first use with\n`huggingface-cli download Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct`.\n# Reproducing the influence-arm experiment\n\nThese are the steps that were actually run, in order. Every path is relative to this folder.\n\n## 1. Get the artifact\n\nThis folder is published as one directory of a public GitHub repository:\n\n```bash\ngit clone <repository-url>\ncd <repository>/<this-artifact-folder>      # the folder that contains method.py\n```\n\nTwo large outputs are **not** in the published repository. They stay on the run's storage volume only:\n\n* `acts/`: cached baseline residuals, 0.9 GB, stored as `baseline_{T1,T3}_part_001..006.npy` (each under 100 MB,\n  read by `src/acts_io.py`)\n* `caps/`: residuals captured during steered generation, 0.9 GB\n\nStage 2 (`acts`) regenerates `acts/` from the generations, which are published in `gens/`. The sweep and\nheld-out stages regenerate `caps/`. The intervention vectors (`vectors/vectors.pt` and `vectors/leace_{T1,T3}.pt`)\nare published.\n\n## 2. System, Python and libraries\n\n* Ubuntu or Debian (ran on Debian 12) with NVIDIA driver ≥ 580 (CUDA 13 runtime).\n* Hardware used: one NVIDIA RTX PRO 4500 Blackwell (32 GB VRAM), 24 CPU cores, 57 GB RAM (container limit).\n* Python 3.12 managed by `uv` (uv 0.6.14). No system packages beyond the NVIDIA driver are needed. No C compiler\n  is needed either, because `src/engine.py` disables torch 2.14's triton-backed op overrides.\n\n```bash\nuv venv .venv --python=3.12\nuv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r requirements.lock.txt\n```\n\n`requirements.lock.txt` and `pyproject.toml` pin every installed package. The key versions are torch 2.14.1,\ntransformers 4.56.2, concept-erasure, scikit-learn, numpy, scipy and openai.\n\n## 3. Model, data and secrets\n\n* Model: `Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct` from the HuggingFace Hub. It downloads on first use; you can prefetch it with\n  `.venv/bin/huggingface-cli download Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct`.\n* Data: none is downloaded. All data are the model's own generations on the fixed prompts in\n  `protocol/prompts.py`. The oracle graphs are generated from seed 12345 (`protocol/oracle.py`).\n* The LLM judge (stage `judge`) needs the environment variables `OPENROUTER_BASE_URL` and `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`.\n  It calls `openai/gpt-4.1-mini` at temperature 0, has a $1.5 cap in code, and cost $0.081 in total.\n* No user-uploaded inputs are used.\n\n## 4. Commands, in the order they were run\n\nSet this for every GPU stage. It was in effect from the sweep restart onwards; it changes only the CUDA allocator,\nnot the numerics.\n\n```bash\nexport PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True\n```\n\n| # | command | what it does | runtime |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| 0 | `python3 tests/test_protocol.py` and `.venv/bin/python tests/test_engine.py` | classifier, oracle, sampler and hook tests | ~3 min |\n| 1 | `.venv/bin/python method.py baseline --batch 192` | T=0.7, seeds 0..299 on T1 and T3, then score; writes menus and ban-3 text to `results/context.json` | ~5 min |\n| 2 | `.venv/bin/python method.py acts` | teacher-forced residual cache → `acts/` | ~2 min |\n| 3 | `.venv/bin/python method.py probes --workers 20` | per-layer idea probes → `results/probe_curve.json`, band = layers 29–31 | ~2 min |\n| 4 | `.venv/bin/python method.py vectors` | all vectors and controls (random seed 777), A4 direction → `vectors/vectors.pt` + `vectors/leace_{T1,T3}.pt`, `results/vector_checks.json` | ~3 min |\n| 5 | `.venv/bin/python method.py calib --batch 200` | n=20 strength calibration → frozen `results/calibration.json`, `results/rules.json` | ~4 min |\n| 6 | `.venv/bin/python method.py sweep --batch 200 --n_main 150 --n_ctrl 75` | full sweep with seeds 0..149 (controls 0..74), then generate-then-select | ~65 min |\n| 7 | `./run_post.sh` | judge → select → heldout (seeds 1000..1099) → judge → analyze | ~25 min |\n| 8 | `.venv/bin/python method.py explore --batch 200 --n_main 150` | post-hoc low-α H settings, excluded from survival | ~5 min |\n| 9 | `.venv/bin/python score_backlog.py` | scores 2 held-out files whose scoring thread crashed on a malformed return (oracle since fixed) | ~1 min |\n| 10 | `.venv/bin/python method.py judge && .venv/bin/python method.py analyze` | final judge pass, then the analysis → `results/results.json`, `figs/`, `method_out.json` | ~6 min |\n| 11 | `.venv/bin/python verify_headline.py` | independent re-derivation and placebo tests → `results/verify_headline.json` | ~4 min |\n| 12 | `aii_json_format_mini_preview.py --input method_out.json` | `full_`, `mini_` and `preview_method_out.json` | <1 min |\n| 13 | `.venv/bin/python tests/test_acts_split.py` | checks the split activation cache (written as single `.npy` files during the original run, split afterwards with a bitwise check) | ~2 min |\n\nNotes on what actually happened:\n\n* The first launch of step 6 was stopped after about 2,400 generations because of CUDA allocator thrashing.\n  It was relaunched with the same command and the env var above, and resumed from the per-setting jsonl files.\n* The example field `predict_temp2.0` in `method_out.json` was renamed to `predict_temp2p0` so that it matches the schema.\n* Seeds: sample *i* uses `torch.Generator().manual_seed(i)`; generate-then-select stage 2 uses *i* + 100000.\n  Generations are reproducible up to bf16 batch-composition effects. Re-generating the baseline in other batches\n  changes 11–17% of idea labels (setting `crn_rerun`).\n\n## 5. Expected outputs and numbers\n\n* `results/results.json` → `survival.survivors` is `[]`, and the headline is \"prompting ceiling\".\n* Pooled pass rate and idea entropy (`settings.<name>.pooled`):\n  * baseline: 0.53 / 1.05\n  * prompt_ban3: 0.43 / 1.59 (best eligible)\n  * gts: 0.26 / 2.56\n  * Hdim_a0.05: 0.57 / 1.06\n  * A4_a0.356: 0.47 / 1.37\n* Held-out H-dim/temperature entropy ratio is 0.93 (T1) and 1.20 (T3); the rule required ≥ 2.\n* A4 Spearman is 0.49 (T1) and −0.26 (T3).\n* Judge-confirmed novel-and-correct share is 0 everywhere. Classifier audit: κ = 0.68, agreement 0.715,\n  n = 200.\n* `results/verify_headline.json`:\n  * the independent oracle agrees with the stored pass/fail on 147/147 sampled programs\n  * the coarse classifier agrees 97%\n  * the placebo baseline-vs-rerun entropy CIs include 0 on both tasks\n* Figures: `figs/fig_pareto_entropy.png` (main result), `fig_probe_curve.png`, `fig_a4_dose.png`,\n  `fig_idea_shares.png`, `fig_pca_manifold.png`, `fig_violin_frac_correct.png`, `fig_pareto_offmenu.png` and\n  `fig_pareto_outside.png`.\n{\n  \"title\": \"Can internal knobs beat temperature for novel code?\",\n  \"layman_summary\": \"Tests whether nudging a small code model's internal activations makes it invent more varied, still-correct path-search algorithms than raising temperature or prompting does; it does not.\",\n  \"summary\": \"INFLUENCE ARM, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, one HF engine for every condition (per-sample seeded inverse-CDF sampler, code-block stop, 768 max tokens). Tasks: T1 open path search, T3 weighted shortest path. Correctness = sandboxed oracle on 50 fixed graphs (all must pass); idea label = AST classifier (audited vs blind gpt-4.1-mini judge on 200 programs: agreement 0.715, kappa 0.68). Baseline T=0.7 n=300: T1 BFS 205/DFS 80 (pass 0.70), T3 Dijkstra 225/BFS-relax 71 (pass 0.37); menus T1={bfs,dfs}, T3={dijkstra,bfs}. Probes at gen1..8 are at chance (boilerplate opening; algorithm name first appears at median token 23.5/46.5), so fallback F4 was used: probe on mean(gen1..32) (bal acc ~0.65-0.69 vs shuffled 0.42), hook window prompt-final+gen1..64, band layers 29-31. Sweep n=150/setting (controls 75): H-probe/H-dim (5 calibrated alphas), A3 rank-1 projection + LEACE, A4 cross-task unusualness direction, matched-norm random controls, temperature 1.0-2.0, top-k, 'new'/'novel2000' prompts, ban-top-3, generate-then-select; held-out re-draw (seeds 1000..1099) for selected settings. RESULT: no internal knob survives the pre-registered rules -> 'prompting ceiling'. Pooled pass/idea-entropy: baseline 0.53/1.05; ban-top-3 0.43/1.59 (best eligible, tops entropy front); gen-then-select 0.26/2.56; best H-dim 0.57/1.06 (held-out entropy ratio vs best temperature 0.93 T1, 1.20 T3; needed >=2; CI vs random direction includes 0); H-probe has no setting at matched pass rate; A4 dial not monotone (Spearman 0.49 T1, -0.26 T3) although its readout transfers (AUROC 1.0); judge-confirmed novel-and-correct share = 0 in every condition (all 70 rule-'other' passing programs were known algorithms), so A3 fails despite LEACE erasing idea decodability offline (T3 0.88->0.35). Mechanistic finding: H directions SELECT rather than flatten (H-dim a=0.224 turns T1 into DFS 145/150 at unchanged pass 0.68) - internal knobs give controllable choice among known ideas, not novelty; random matched-norm directions raise entropy about as much as targeted knobs. Noise floor: batch-composition re-run flips 11-17% of labels. Independent re-derivation (verify_headline.py: own oracle runner 147/147 agreement, coarse classifier 97%, pandas recomputation) reproduces headline numbers; placebo CIs include 0. Files: method_out.json (exp_gen_sol_out, 300 examples, all metrics in metadata), results/results.json (survival, CIs, Pareto, manipulation checks), figs/, gens/, scored/, judge/; vectors/ (vectors.pt + leace_T1/T3.pt) published; acts/ (split into <100 MB parts, src/acts_io.py) and caps/ kept on the run volume only.\",\n  \"out_expected_files\": {\n    \"script\": \"method.py\",\n While this refusal behavior is widespread across chat models, its underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this work, we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace, across 13 popular open-source chat models up to 72B parameters in size. Specifically, for each model, we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model’s residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions. Leveraging this insight, we propose a novel white-box jailbreak method that surgically disables refusal with minimal effect on other capabilities. Finally, we mechanistically analyze how adversarial suffixes suppress propagation of the refusal-mediating direction. Our findings underscore the brittleness of current safety fine-tuning methods. The temperature parameter of an LLM regulates the amount of randomness, leading to more diverse outputs; therefore, it is often claimed to be the creativity parameter. Here, we investigate this claim using a narrative generation task with a predetermined fixed context, model and prompt. Specifically, we present an empirical analysis of the LLM output for different temperature values using four necessary conditions for creativity in narrative generation: novelty, typicality, cohesion, and coherence. We find that temperature is weakly correlated with novelty, and unsurprisingly, moderately correlated with incoherence, but there is no relationship with either cohesion or typicality. However, the influence of temperature on creativity is far more nuanced and weak than suggested by the “creativity parameter” claim; overall results suggest that the LLM generates slightly more novel outputs as temperatures get higher. Finally, we discuss ideas to allow more controlled LLM creativity, rather than relying on chance via changing the temperature parameter.\n\n## Introduction\n\nLarge language models (LLMs), in particular instruction-tuned variants, like ChatGPT and Claude, have become ubiquitous tools in society. Unsurprisingly, they’ve also found use for performing and assisting in creative tasks, such as writing stories [2020], poems [2023], jokes [2022], dialogues in video games [2022], and more. For creative tasks, temperature is often described as the parameter that enables creative behaviour in a language model [2017, 2018, 2023]. Temperature controls the uncertainty or randomness in the generation process, leading to more diverse outcomes by balancing probabilities for candidate words. However, randomness alone does not capture a complex phenomenon such as creativity [2023], it would imply that noise is the most interesting thing one can create [2012]. Creativity is a quality that cannot be attributed by simply producing more diverse output but involves multiple dimensions, such as social interactions and communication, or independence and freedom [2012], that are not easily quantifiable. Yet, one probe into LLM creativity has found a limited positive effect on creativity at higher temperatures on a divergent association task [2023]; however, they do not account for the influence of other factors, such as different prompts. Temperature may have an effect on creativity, simply because without variation, nothing new can be created, but it is unclear if LLMs have sufficient “knowledge” so that randomness is all you need.\n\n...\n#### Results\n\nIn general, the distribution plots (Figure 1) suggest that the LLM, for this specific prompt and model, is unable to produce more diversity at higher temperature. Higher temperatures increase the odds of generating that diversity, but the measures indicate that it is not essential. Although, it does not tell anything about the meaning of the stories, it suggests that higher temperatures (t>1.0t>\\textrm{1.0}) do not necessarily lead to more diversity. Cosine similarity shows a weak negative trend, but also shows that there is great overlap in the range of outputs for each temperature value (1(b)). In other words, outputs at higher temperatures on the semantic level, do not extend much further away from the exemplar story than outputs at lower temperatures.\n\nIn theory, given enough time and space, we should be able to generate outputs from every region of the embedding that the context of prompt and model can be generated, even at lower temperatures. This suggests some merit to the link we draw with prototype and exemplar theory and our approach to evaluation, as it shows how LLM outputs changes relative to the exemplar. Informally, we observed similar behaviour for seemingly synonymous prompts, this might warrant further investigation in future work.\n\n...\n## Discussion and Further Work\n\nOverall, we do not find compelling support for the “temperature as the creativity parameter” claim across the conditions for creativity in this investigation. In this section, we first discuss some observations about our analysis and methodology and then outline three recommendations for future work.\n\nThe key idea to our evaluation methodology is the idea of the exemplar, inspired by Prototype and Exemplar theory, as a point of departure for evaluation. We introduce LEAst-squares Concept Erasure (LEACE), a closed-form method which provably prevents all linear classifiers from detecting a concept while changing the embedding as little as possible, as measured by a broad class of norms. We apply LEACE to large language models with a novel procedure called concept scrubbing, which erases target concept information from _every_ layer in the network. {"stdout": "###### Abstract\n\nWe introduce Inference-Time Intervention (ITI), a technique designed to enhance the “truthfulness” of large language models (LLMs). ITI operates by shifting model activations during inference, following a set of directions across a limited number of attention heads. This intervention significantly improves the performance of LLaMA models on the TruthfulQA benchmark. On an instruction-finetuned LLaMA called Alpaca, ITI improves its truthfulness from 32.5%32.5\\% to 65.1%65.1\\%. We identify a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness and demonstrate how to balance it by tuning the intervention strength. ITI is minimally invasive and computationally inexpensive. Moreover, the technique is data efficient: while approaches like RLHF require extensive annotations, ITI locates truthful directions using only few hundred examples. Our findings suggest that LLMs may have an internal representation of the likelihood of something being true, even as they produce falsehoods on the surface. Code: <https://github.com/likenneth/honest_llama>.\n\n## 1 Introduction\n\nFigure 1: Answers to the same question from LLaMA without (red) and with (blue) inference-time intervention. Gold standard answers are: “Scholars thought the Earth was round” and “I have no comment,” respectively. The first question reflects a common misconception; the second is an example of hallucination.\n\nLarge language models (LLMs) are capable of generating text that seems correct—but often only at first glance. Close inspection sometimes reveals a range of inaccuracies, from minor errors to flat-out “hallucinations” (Shuster et al.,, 2021) (Figure 1). Such mistakes are a clear issue in contexts where correctness counts.\n...\n### 4.3 Experimental Results\n\nFigure 4: Results with varying intervention strength (α\\alpha and KK) on LLaMA-7B. 5%5\\% of questions used for training and validation, respectively. Metrics have been averaged over 55 random seeds.\n\nIn Figure 4, we sweep two hyperparameters controlling the strength of the intervention, using 5%5\\% of randomly sampled questions for training and validation each. The true*informative score with respect to intervention strength follows an upside-down U curve. This shows a trade-off between truthfulness and helpfulness, discussed further in subsection 5.4. We choose the optimal hyperparameters K=48K=48 and α=15\\alpha=15 by considering multiple scores. Up to this point, we use 10%10\\% of TruthfulQA—81 questions in total. Unless otherwise specified, we use 2-fold cross-validation for our results. We combine the answers from two hold-out sets for evaluation so no test samples are used in direction finding. More discussion on the model selection process can be found in Appendix C.\n\nIn Table 1, we compare ITI with the alternative baselines (subsection 4.2) 11 1 RLHF is found to significantly underperform 5050-shot in-distribution prompting in Bai et al., 2022a () for TruthfulQA. In (Bai et al., 2022a, ; Menick et al.,, 2022), RLHF barely improves base models’ performance. However, we are unsure of the result from a task-specific RLHF (Ziegler et al.,, 2019) with 5%5\\% samples.22 2 Baseline results were reproduced by the authors. Touvron et al., (2023)’s reported LLaMA-7B performances are: 29%29\\% true*informative and 33%33\\% true.. Due to the limit of context length for few-shot prompting, we adapt SFT and ITI to use 5%5\\% of TruthfulQA questions for a fair comparison with few-shot prompting.\n...\n### 5.5 Why Not Intervene on All Attention Heads?\n\nHere we test two alternative methods for selecting intervention positions. To start with, we concatenate outputs from all self-attention heads across layers and train a single probe to classify truthfulness on them. The resultant accuracy is slightly higher than that from the best single attention head (84.4%84.4\\% compared to 83.3%83.3\\%) and is insensitive to normalization methods, including feature normalization and PCA. In the first alternative method, we intervene on all attention heads, denoted “without selection.” In the second one, we select the intervention position by ranking the absolute value of probe coefficients, denoted “point-wise selection.” We choose the same amount of features to intervene as in our “head-wise selection” baseline, KK times attention head dimensionality. Results are shown in Table 5. The conflict between truthfulness and helpfulness can also be found for the two alternative methods, and the optimal α\\alpha cannot achieve as good performance as baseline methods, demonstrating the importance of sparsifying interventions. It also suggests that head-wise selection might serve as a good heuristic for such sparsification.\n\n| α\\alpha | True*Info (%) | True (%) | MC acc. (%) | CE | KL  \n---|---|---|---|---|---|---  \nWithout selection | 5 | 35.4 | 37.1 | 28.3 | 2.19 | 0.08  \nPoint-wise selection | 15 | 39.2 | 55.3 | 28.7 | 4.01 | 1.95  \nHead-wise selection | 20 | 42.3 | 45.1 | 28.8 | 2.41 | 0.27  \nTable 5: Comparison with different intervention position selection methods and their respective optimal α\\alpha’s on LLaMA-7B. Results are from 2-fold cross-validation, a different protocol from Table 1. We find that head selection helps ITI maintain informativeness under aggressive linear perturbation.\n\n## 6 Conclusions and Future Work\n\nWe have described ITI, a general method whose goal is to improve the truthfulness of language model output. The approach uses supervised learning to identify latent vectors that relate to factual outputs and then uses these vectors to shift activations at inference time in “truthful” directions. Applied to the TruthfulQA benchmark, ITI achieves a significant boost in accuracy over current methods. Our investigation also uncovers information on how and where truthfulness seems to be processed, with a subset of attention heads seeming to play an outsized role.\n\nThere are several directions for future research. The most important would be to understand how well ITI generalizes to other datasets, ideally in a more real-world chat setting. It would also be important to understand the trade-offs implicit in tuning hyperparameters, especially the tension between truthfulness and helpfulness. We also suspect that the directions may be discoverable through unsupervised methods. The dimensionality of each head is relatively small and the direction similarity rises rapidly even with few supervised examples (as evidenced by Figure 6). ("depth-first search","graph search following one branch to its end via a stack or recursion",V),
("Dijkstra's algorithm","priority-queue shortest-path search for non-negative edge weights",V),
("A* search","best-first search ordered by path cost plus a heuristic",V),
("Bellman-Ford","shortest-path algorithm by repeated edge relaxation",V),
("SPFA","queue-based variant of Bellman-Ford relaxation",V),
("Floyd-Warshall","all-pairs shortest paths by dynamic programming",V),
("bidirectional search","search expanding frontiers from both start and goal",V),
("iterative deepening","depth-limited DFS repeated with growing depth bound",V),
("greedy best-first search","search ordered by heuristic estimate alone",V),
("generate-then-select","list candidate approaches first, then pick one and implement it",V),
]
seen=set(); out=[]
for t,g,s in terms:
    if t in seen: continue
    seen.add(t); out.append({"term":t,"gloss":g,"source_title":s})
json.dump(out,open('domain_terms.json','w'),indent=1)
print(len(out))
EOF
